question: Three lots in an auction catalogue, worded by a house's own glossary. Which ones claim the master drew it?
answer: Only the first, and even that is an opinion. Auction houses grade their confidence in small words before a name. Eric Hebborn exploited that: he drew in old masters' manners on old paper, never signed, and let experts supply the names; a wrong attribution, he argued, was their error. He later claimed 1,000 fakes.
move: A claim can mislead even when nobody wrote a false word.
ask: Where have I misled someone lately without saying anything false?

scene.body: Lot 41: Anthony van Dyck, Head of a man. Lot 42: Attributed to Anthony van Dyck, Head of a man. Lot 43: Manner of Anthony van Dyck, Head of a man.

phrases.plain: Lot 41: by van Dyck, in our opinion
phrases.why: The bare name is the strongest claim a catalogue makes, and still an opinion.

phrases.plain: Probably by, in whole or in part,
phrases.why: The house's glossary says probably. A hedge you can see in the estimate.

phrases.plain: Not by him, and of a later date:
phrases.why: In his style, made later. It names the master without claiming him.

scene.ask: One phrase names the master and says he didn't draw it. Which?
scene.watch: In a catalogue the claim is the small words before the name.

reference: Eric Hebborn, Drawn to Trouble: The Forging of an Artist, Mainstream Publishing, 1991
